nameStory: Tetrabaena gets its name from the Greek words 'tetra' meaning four and 'baena' meaning to go or walk, referring to how these tiny organisms move through water as a group of exactly four cells. The species name 'socialis' means social in Latin, highlighting how these four cells live and work together as one of nature's simplest communities.
description: Tetrabaena socialis is a microscopic green algae that represents one of the simplest forms of multicellular life on Earth. This tiny organism consists of just four green cells that stick together and swim through freshwater as a coordinated unit. Each cell is equipped with two whip-like tails called flagella that beat together to propel the four-cell colony through the water. You'll need a microscope to see these remarkable little creatures, as they're far too small to spot with the naked eye.

idTips.label: Four-cell structure
idTips.description: Always consists of exactly four round, green cells arranged in a flat, diamond or square pattern when viewed under a microscope

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves through water with a distinctive rolling or spinning motion as all eight flagella (two per cell) beat in coordination

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Cells appear vibrant green due to chlorophyll, similar to the color of fresh grass or spinach leaves

idTips.label: Flagella movement
idTips.description: Two thin, whip-like flagella extend from each cell and create rapid, wave-like motions visible under magnification

idTips.label: Colony coordination
idTips.description: The four cells move as a single unit rather than independently, maintaining their formation while swimming

habitat: Tetrabaena socialis lives in clean freshwater environments throughout New England, including ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. Look for them in areas with good water quality where other green algae and aquatic plants thrive. They're most commonly found in the upper layers of water where sunlight can reach them for photosynthesis.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight increases, making this a good time to find them in freshwater samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when warm temperatures and long days provide ideal conditions for growth and reproduction in ponds and lakes.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall but populations may decline as temperatures drop and daylight hours decrease.
seasonality.winter: Populations are greatly reduced or dormant in frozen or very cold water, though some may survive in deeper, unfrozen areas.

funFact: Tetrabaena socialis is like nature's first experiment with teamwork - these four cells gave up their independence millions of years ago and now can't survive alone, making them a living example of how cooperation led to more complex life forms including ourselves!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, Tetrabaena might be confused with other small colonial green algae, but the key is counting cells - if you see exactly four cells moving together, you've found Tetrabaena. Remember 'four-baena' to keep the number straight.
contextualKnowledge: While called an 'algae,' Tetrabaena is actually more closely related to single-celled organisms than to the large seaweeds we typically think of as algae. It represents an evolutionary stepping stone between single-celled and truly multicellular life forms.
compareHints: Tetrabaena is unique among New England's microscopic organisms for its consistent four-cell structure. While other colonial algae may form groups of various sizes, Tetrabaena always maintains exactly four cells. This makes it quite distinct from similar flagellated algae that either live alone or form larger, variable-sized colonies.
